group_assessment.weighting: Review and hypothesis paper of glucose and glycogen metabolism in epilepsy (FDG-PET, 13C-glucose labelling, rodent seizure models, two human biopsy and microdialysis series). It contributes background on fuel supply during seizures and on starvation before seizures; it contains one original figure from the authors' earlier mouse data. Not a WWOX system and not a feeding or fluid study. The text contains no mention of GSK3 or WWOX (a string count over the rendered text returned 0 for both), so the selection file's link to the GSK3B arm is not carried by this paper.

entries.proposition: It is a hypothesis and review paper with no primary data.
entries.snippet: As this is a hypothesis paper, there were no primary data used, and no ethical approval and no patient consent were needed.
entries.anchor: Statements relating to ethics and integrity

entries.proposition: In rats starved for 24 h before bicuculline seizures, glucose stayed low, glycogen was nearly depleted and did not recover.
entries.snippet: Importantly, when rats were starved for 24 h prior to seizure induction, blood and brain glucose levels remained low, glycogen levels were nearly depleted and did not recover, and glucose‐6‐P levels were reduced.
entries.anchor: Brain glycogen levels in epilepsy models and patients, last paragraph

entries.proposition: The review states that, in the 24 h starved rats of one cited study, the effects of preseizure starvation indicate fuel availability from the blood is essential for brain energetics and glycogen replenishment.
entries.snippet: These effects of preseizure starvation indicate fuel availability from the blood is essential for brain energetics and glycogen replenishment.
entries.anchor: Brain glycogen levels in epilepsy models and patients, last paragraph

contradicts_locator.what_changed: scope limited to the cited starvation experiment

entries.proposition: Interictal brain glucose is not reduced in the studies compiled in Table 1.
entries.snippet: The results from different studies (Table 1) strongly support the conclusion that brain glucose levels are not reduced interictally and that brain glucose deficiency is an unlikely cause of interictal hypometabolism in animal models for epilepsy.
entries.anchor: Brain glucose levels and glucose utilization, para 3

entries.proposition: In healthy adults acute hypoglycaemia raised glycogen and repeated hypoglycaemia blunted that response, which the authors take as glycogen responding to fuel deficit.
entries.snippet: that was blunted with repeated episodes of hypoglycemia, 69 supporting the possibility that glycogen levels respond to fuel deficits during hypoglycemia and seizures.

entries.proposition: Brain-specific glycogen synthase-deficient mice were more susceptible to seizures, cited as support.
entries.snippet: Furthermore, absence of glycogen seems to promote seizures, as brain‐specific glycogen synthase‐deficient mice showed increased susceptibility to seizures.

entries.proposition: The central claim is a hypothesis: glycogen use adapts to recurrent seizures, with interictal glycogenolysis lowering FDG signal.
entries.snippet: We propose that glycogen levels and utilization adapt to recurrent seizures in epileptic brains, with increased concentrations and unrecognized functional roles during interictal periods.

entries.proposition: The authors say that evidence on glycogen turnover between seizures is scarce and that more research is needed.
entries.snippet: Elevated interictal glycogen content may appear to contradict its proposed role in fueling spiking or high‐frequency oscillations and managing oxidative stress, but we emphasize that there is a paucity of information regarding glycogen turnover and regulation during the interictal period.
entries.anchor: Glycogen and seizure generation, last paragraph

entries.proposition: The proposed benefit of auxiliary fuels (ketones, MCT, pyruvate) is stated as an expectation.
entries.snippet: Supplemental oxidative fuel is expected to reduce glucose utilization and spare glucose for glycolytic production of ATP and for flux into the pentose phosphate shunt in both neurons and astrocytes
entries.anchor: Glycogen and seizure generation, final paragraph

entries.proposition: Stress, alerting and seizures release norepinephrine, which the authors list as a trigger of glycogen mobilisation that could bias PET and labelling data.
entries.snippet: First, stress, alerting, and seizures trigger norepinephrine release to blood and can activate the locus coeruleus to cause norepinephrine release in brain

entries.proposition: Figure 1 shows plasma glucose 13C enrichment similar between groups and lower enrichment in G6P, F6P, DHAP and PEP in the status epilepticus group (asterisks), with total pools unchanged.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 1: percent 13C enrichment, plasma glucose about 14.4 (no SE) and 12.6 (SE) with no asterisk; hippocampal G6P about 13.3 versus 10.3, F6P about 13.3 versus 10.4, DHAP about 15.6 versus 13.0 and PEP about 14.9 versus 11.9 with asterisks, F16BP and PYR without asterisks.

experimental_context.system: chronic stage of the mouse pilocarpine model, hippocampus, 13C-glucose injection, interictal

entries.proposition: The author group's own back-of-envelope calculation says glycogen could carry a 20% fall in glucose use for about 90 min in mouse hippocampus.
entries.snippet: Based on glycogen content of ~13 μmol/g reported in healthy mouse hippocampus, 88 this amount would be able to sustain ~90 min of a reduction in CMRGLC by providing energy from glycogenolysis.
entries.anchor: Glycogenolysis reduces glucose utilization in astrocytes, para 3
